article.title: Mojo Reaches Stable 1.0 as Modular Locks In API Guarantees After Three Years of Beta Churn
article.summary: Modular shipped Mojo 1.0 on August 11, days after Qualcomm completed its acquisition of the company, promising the language will no longer shift beneath developers.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Modular released Mojo 1.0 on August 11, 2026, as part of its Modular 26.5 update, [officially declaring](https://www.modular.com/blog/modular-26-5-mojo-1-0-is-here) that "the Mojo language officially reaches 1.0: a milestone the language has been building toward since its first release in 2023." The stable release lands roughly three months after [Mojo's 1.0 beta shipped](/article/2026-05/25-mojo-10-beta-arrives-as-modular-declares-the-ai-native-systems-language-feature-complete) and just weeks after Qualcomm completed its purchase of Modular, the startup behind the language, [previously reported](/article/2026-06/25-qualcomm-to-buy-ai-software-startup-modular-for-about-39-billion-taking-aim-at-nvidias-cuda-moat) as an all-stock deal worth about $3.9 billion.

## What We Know

### A Stability Commitment After Years of Breaking Changes

Mojo's central promise with 1.0 is that the language will stop shifting under developers who build on it. As [Modular's blog post](https://www.modular.com/blog/modular-26-5-mojo-1-0-is-here) states, "During the 1.x timeframe, changes should primarily be additive, giving developers confidence that the language will not continually shift beneath them." The company frames this as a readiness signal rather than a marketing milestone: "We are making that commitment today because Mojo is ready: it is no longer just a language we are developing; it is a language we rely on every day in production."

According to [XenoSpectrum](https://xenospectrum.com/en/mojo-1-0-stability-open-source/), the stability guarantee is not blanket coverage: "Stability guarantees are limited to explicitly marked APIs, and homework remains regarding the ABI, toolchain, and open-sourcing of the compiler." Within the standard library, the outlet reports that "traits that are fully stable include `Deinitable`, `Movable`, `Copyable`, and `ImplicitlyCopyable`, while `Array`, `List`, `Span`, `String`, `Bool`, and `Optional` have begun stabilization only for some of their APIs."

### What Changed Since the Beta

Mojo's 1.0 beta, which shipped in May, had already deprecated the `fn` keyword and turned on default bounds checking. The stable release adds further language cleanup: [Linuxiac reports](https://linuxiac.com/mojo-1-0-programming-language-officially-released/) that "variables are now consistently declared using `var`," and that Mojo has moved to a single `Pointer` type, down from the four pointer variants offered in the beta. Python-style lambda syntax also lands for the first time — [XenoSpectrum notes](https://xenospectrum.com/en/mojo-1-0-stability-open-source/) that "developers coming from Python gain `lambda` expressions, allowing single-expression anonymous closures."

Developer-experience work also shipped alongside the language changes. Linuxiac reports that "the language server has received substantial work, improving the editing experience in VS Code," and that Mojo now "detects invalidated references, including when list operations invalidate existing references." On performance, XenoSpectrum reports that improvements to Python interoperability meant "execution paths involving repeated `a + b` or `a < b` operations became about 12 times faster."

### Qualcomm's Acquisition Has Closed

Mojo's creator, Chris Lattner — described by [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/12/modulars-mojo-programming-language-hits-10-milestone/5286545) as the "creator of LLVM, the Clang compiler, the Swift programming language, and the MLIR compiler infrastructure" — built Mojo through Modular, the startup he co-founded, which The Register confirms "was acquired by Qualcomm in June." According to [Techzine](https://www.techzine.eu/news/devops/143570/mojo-programming-language-reaches-version-1-0/) and independently confirmed by [XenoSpectrum](https://xenospectrum.com/en/mojo-1-0-stability-open-source/), Qualcomm completed the acquisition on July 29, 2026.

The closing has raised questions among developers about whether Mojo and its MAX platform can remain vendor-neutral under a chipmaker's ownership. Asked by The Register about the risk of interference from rivals such as Nvidia or AMD following the takeover, Lattner said: "They both contribute an incredible amount to open source code. So I don't expect there to be any problem here." Techzine reports that Modular has stated "the acquisition does not change" the language's independence commitment.

### The Compiler Is Still Closed

Mojo's standard library has been open source for some time, released under the Apache License v2.0 with LLVM Exceptions, according to The Register. The compiler and toolchain, however, remain proprietary. Modular reiterated in its own announcement that "our commitment remains unchanged – we will open source the Mojo compiler and toolchain in 2026," and Techzine reports that Modular is "hosting ModCon in San Francisco on August 18" to share further plans. XenoSpectrum frames the open-sourcing as the real test of the vendor-neutrality pledge, writing that "vendor neutrality can only truly be measured once outside parties can verify the implementation and licensing for themselves."

### Community Growth Since the Standard Library Opened

Modular says contributor activity has scaled substantially since the standard library was opened up: "Since we open-sourced the standard library, nearly 200 contributors have landed more than 1,100 pull requests, changing over 200,000 lines of code," according to the company's own announcement.

## What We Don't Know

Modular has not published a specific date within 2026 for opening the compiler and toolchain source code, beyond the general commitment and the hint — reported by The Register — that an announcement could come at the ModCon conference. XenoSpectrum's reporting suggests the stability guarantee's practical scope is still narrower than "the whole language," since it currently applies only to APIs explicitly marked stable, with the ABI and toolchain still described as unfinished work. Neither Modular nor the outlets covering the release have detailed how Qualcomm's ownership will affect Modular's commercial roadmap or pricing for its MAX platform going forward.

## Analysis

Mojo's path to 1.0 has been unusually public: three years of iterative language changes, a beta in May that broke existing code on purpose to clear the way for a stable core, and now a release that arrives within weeks of its parent company changing hands. Shipping the stability guarantee so soon after the Qualcomm deal closed reads as an attempt to reassure developers on two fronts at once — that the language itself won't move under them, and that new ownership won't either. The remaining test, as XenoSpectrum's framing suggests, is whether Modular actually opens the compiler this year: until outside parties can inspect that code, claims of vendor neutrality rest on Modular's word rather than on anything the ecosystem can independently verify.
